nary_nodes.label: Google pauses Nano Banana 2 in Google Earth
evidence: Less than 48 hours after the tech giant announced the integration of its AI image generator Nano Banana 2 into Google Earth, it said it was pausing the feature "while we work on implementing stronger guardrails".
nary_nodes.type_definition: An event where a software feature is temporarily disabled or paused.
nary_nodes.type_justification: No candidate models this event; a new subclass of Event is required.

nary_nodes.label: BBC Verify tests generate fake images with Nano Banana 2
evidence: A collapsed Eiffel Tower, a sinkhole swallowing the Great Pyramid of Giza and Russian tanks in Ukraine's capital were among the images BBC Verify was able to create when testing the feature, which initially launched on Thursday.
nary_nodes.type_definition: An event in which a tool is evaluated or tested.
nary_nodes.type_justification: Existing candidates are unrelated user‑interaction types; a new Event subclass fits.

nary_nodes.label: Henk van Ess highlights misuse risks of Nano Banana 2
evidence: Before it was paused, AI and misinformation expert Henk van Ess highlighted the risks the feature posed, by creating fake images of a non‑existent nuclear power plant in Iran, a refugee camp on the US‑Mexico border and a fake hospital in Gaza with a bomb crater next to it.
nary_nodes.type_definition: An event where an expert draws attention to potential risks of a technology.
nary_nodes.type_justification: No suitable existing class; a new Event subclass captures the meaning.

nary_nodes.label: Google adds invisible watermarks to AI‑generated content
evidence: Google said AI content created by its tools contain invisible watermarks to indicate that they are fake or manipulated, adding that anyone who is "unsure about an image" can check it using the Gemini chatbot app or use the Lens feature in its search.
nary_nodes.type_definition: An event where invisible watermarks are added to AI‑generated media.
nary_nodes.type_justification: Existing candidates do not represent this; a new Event subclass is needed.

nary_nodes.label: External AI detection tools sometimes fail to identify fake Google Earth images
evidence: Generally, BBC Verify's tests found this is effective with images generated by the new feature. But we also found it was possible to circumnavigate these checks and trick Gemini into saying these fake Google Earth images are real.
nary_nodes.type_definition: An event where AI detection tools fail to identify manipulated content.
nary_nodes.type_justification: No candidate matches; a new Event subclass best describes the situation.

nary_nodes.label: Experts warn Nano Banana 2 could spread misinformation
evidence: Google has rolled back its new AI tool that allowed people to create fake images on top of its satellite imagery, following a BBC Verify report in which experts raised concerns about misuse and the potential to spread misinformation.

nary_nodes.label: Google saw people sharing screenshots that violate policies
evidence: In its statement on Friday, Google said it had seen "people sharing screenshots of generated imagery that appear to violate our policies".

nary_nodes.label: Forgery inherits credibility of the map it was born on
evidence: He said Google had allowed "invented" imagery to be "welded to genuine coordinates, drawn on genuine imagery". "The forgery does not have to look convincing on its own. It inherits the credibility of the map it was born on," van Ess added.

nary_nodes.label: Google says AI content contains invisible watermarks
evidence: Google said AI content created by its tools contain invisible watermarks to indicate that they are fake or manipulated, adding that anyone who is "unsure about an image" can check it using the Gemini chatbot app or use the Lens feature in its search.

nary_nodes.label: Fake imagery in conflict zones could be destabilising
evidence: AI‑detection researcher Henry Ajder told BBC Verify the creation of fake imagery in conflict zones could prove particularly "destabilising" when events are fast‑moving and information is scarce.

nary_nodes.label: Falsified satellite imagery erodes public trust
evidence: "This is potentially particularly damaging to public trust because satellite imagery has historically been seen as an especially trustworthy source of data," Bill Greer, a geospatial analyst and co‑founder of the non‑profit satellite service Common Space, told BBC Verify.
